client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away a few weeks ago. I keep zoning out at work, like I'll be in the middle of a task and suddenly realize I've just been staring at my screen for twenty minutes thinking about her. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: Thank you for being here and for taking that step, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — that kind of courage in the face of doubt says a lot about how much you want to find your way through this. The way you're describing those moments at work, suddenly surfacing from thoughts of her, sounds like grief quietly pulling you back to her, which makes complete sense given how recent this loss is. We can work together gently at whatever pace feels right for you, and even if talking doesn't "fix" anything, it can help you understand what you're carrying and find small ways to carry it a little more steadily.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not totally sure "courage" is the right word — it feels more like desperation, honestly. The zoning out has been happening more and more, and my boss already made a comment about a deadline I missed, so I kind of had to do something. I guess what I'm struggling with is that I don't really see how talking about her is going to help me focus better at work.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of urgency — really reflects what you're describing: this isn't abstract for you, there's real pressure mounting and it makes sense that you'd need something practical, not just emotional. You're right to name that distinction between courage and desperation, and honestly, desperation can be its own kind of honest motivation. What I'd gently offer is that the zoning out *is* the grief — your mind is trying to process something enormous — and understanding that connection is actually where we start to find some relief, both emotionally and in terms of your focus.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, I can see the logic in what you're saying — that the zoning out and the grief are connected — but I guess I'm not sure how just "understanding" that is supposed to make it stop happening. Like, I already know I'm sad about losing her, that's not news to me. What I don't know is how to be in a meeting and not suddenly be somewhere else entirely.
therapist: That's a really fair pushback, and your voice carries a kind of strained urgency that tells me this isn't just a theoretical frustration — you need something that actually works in the room, in the moment. So let's get concrete: one CBT-based approach is learning to use brief "grounding anchors" when you feel your mind starting to drift — a specific physical sensation, a deliberate breath, a single word you say internally — that gently signals your brain to return to the present without fighting the grief. It doesn't make the sadness disappear, but it gives you a small tool to work with in those moments rather than just being swept away by them.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, that sounds reasonable in theory, but I feel like by the time I even notice I've zoned out, I've already been gone for a while — like it's not something I catch in the moment, it's more like I come back to the surface and realize I've lost twenty minutes. So I'm not sure I'd even have the chance to use an anchor before it's too late.
therapist: You're speaking quickly and there's a real tension in what you're describing — like you're trying hard to problem-solve your way out of something that keeps slipping through your fingers before you can even grab it. That's actually a really important observation about yourself, and it shifts the approach: rather than catching the drift *as it happens*, we can work on building in *proactive* structure — things like brief intentional check-ins every few minutes during meetings, or a subtle physical cue beforehand that primes your brain to stay anchored. It's less about reacting to the wave and more about changing the conditions before it builds.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Setting a timer or something to check in with myself every few minutes — I don't know, that feels like it might actually make things worse, like I'd be so focused on watching for the drift that I'd just be more anxious the whole time. And honestly, the meetings aren't even the hardest part — it's more when I'm working alone at my desk that I really lose track of time. I guess I'm also just wondering if there's something deeper going on that these techniques aren't really getting at, like maybe I feel guilty that I wasn't there when she actually passed.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, high, with something that sounds like it's been held in for a while — makes me think that last part, about the guilt, took something to say out loud. That feels like the real weight underneath everything, and your instinct that the techniques weren't quite reaching it was right. Grief mixed with guilt is one of the heaviest combinations there is, and I'd really like to gently explore that with you — because often that guilt is built on thoughts that feel absolutely true but don't hold up when we look at them carefully together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, it did take something to say — I've barely even admitted that to myself, let alone out loud to someone else. I was living across the country when she died, and I kept telling myself I'd visit soon, and then suddenly there was no more soon. I guess I'm a little worried that if we "look at it carefully," you're just going to tell me the guilt isn't rational or that I did my best, and I'm not sure I'm ready to hear that, because part of me feels like I deserve to feel bad about it.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now, combined with what you just shared, tells me this is hitting something very deep and very raw — and I want you to know I'm not going to rush in and take the guilt away from you, because that's not my job and it wouldn't be honest. What I'd gently offer is that there's a difference between *examining* the guilt and *dismissing* it — we're not here to decide you shouldn't feel bad, but to understand what that guilt is actually saying to you, because sometimes it carries something important about how much you loved her. You get to keep that love, and we can look at the guilt together without me trying to talk you out of your own experience.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That actually... helps a little, hearing you say that. I think what I've been afraid of is someone just patting me on the head and telling me it's fine, because it doesn't feel fine, and having someone dismiss it would almost feel like dismissing how much she meant to me. But I'm still not totally sure what "examining" it even looks like — like, are we just going to talk about the timeline of what happened, because I'm not sure I can do that without completely falling apart.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, even as you're saying something so vulnerable, tells me you're holding this very carefully — and I want to hold it carefully too. Examining the guilt doesn't mean walking through a painful timeline of events; it's more about gently noticing the thoughts that are driving it, like "I should have visited sooner," and asking what that belief is resting on — not to erase it, but to understand it more fully. And if you do start to fall apart at some point, that's okay — falling apart in here is actually allowed, and it doesn't mean we've gone too far.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think "I should have visited sooner" is probably the core of it, yeah — that thought is pretty much on a loop in my head. But when you say "what is that belief resting on," I'm not sure what you mean, because it feels like it's resting on just... facts. I didn't visit, and now I can't. I'm not sure how you examine something that's just true.
therapist: Your voice carries something tight and strained right now, like you're bracing against something — and what you just said is actually one of the most important distinctions in this kind of work. You're right that "I didn't visit" is a fact, but "I *should* have visited sooner" is an interpretation layered on top of that fact — it contains an assumption that you *could* have known there was no more time, that a reasonable version of you would have acted differently. And that's exactly what's worth examining: not whether the facts are true, but whether the story you're telling about what those facts *mean* about you is the only possible story.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me can follow the logic — like, I genuinely didn't know she was going to die when she did, nobody told me it was urgent. But there's another part of me that keeps saying I should have just known, like a good granddaughter would have felt it somehow and made the trip happen regardless. I'm not sure I can fully accept that I was just a "reasonable person making reasonable choices" when the result was that I never got to say goodbye.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now, even as the words themselves feel almost measured, tells me there's something urgent and painful pressing against the surface here — and I want to name what I'm hearing: you're holding two things at once, the logical you and the part that believes a *good* granddaughter would have somehow *sensed* it. That second belief — that love should have made you psychic — is worth sitting with, because it's not actually a standard you'd apply to anyone else you love, and yet you're holding yourself to it completely. Not getting to say goodbye is a real and painful loss on top of the loss itself, and you're allowed to grieve that specifically — but "I didn't know" and "I was a good granddaughter" can both be true at the same time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That thing you said about not applying that standard to anyone else — that actually stopped me for a second, because you're right, if a friend told me she hadn't visited her grandmother and then lost her, I would never think "she should have sensed it was time." But somehow when it's me, it feels completely different, like the rules just don't apply the same way. I'm not sure I can just decide to believe both things are true at once — it feels like letting myself off the hook, and I'm not ready to do that yet.
therapist: The softness in your voice even as you're speaking quickly tells me this landed somewhere real and tender — and I want to be clear that believing both things doesn't mean letting yourself off the hook, it means being as fair to yourself as you would be to someone you love. You don't have to be ready to fully accept it yet; noticing that you hold yourself to a different standard than you'd hold your friend is already something, and we can just stay with that observation for now without forcing it into a conclusion. That double standard — that's not justice, that's grief turning into punishment, and you deserve to at least question whether you've earned that punishment.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
